title: Inkjet printer: motors, rods, belts and encoders
summary: Offices and schools are full of dead inkjet printers. Each holds two or more DC or stepper motors, a polished steel guide rod, timing belts and pulleys, an optical encoder, gears, springs and a 24–32 V power supply. About 15 minutes with a screwdriver.

steps.text: Unplug the printer and leave it 5 minutes. Pull the ink cartridges out and bag them: ink stains everything.
steps.warn: An internal power supply board can hold a mains-level charge for a few minutes after unplugging.

steps.text: Take off the paper trays. Find the screws: under rubber feet, behind the cartridge door, at the back and under the scanner lid. Remove them all.
All-in-one models: lift off the scanner lid and scanner bed first. It holds a light bar, a small motor, a belt and a rod of its own.
Pop the outer shell off. Start at the back and work forward, pressing clips in with a flat screwdriver.
steps.warn: Plastic clips snap into sharp shards and the frame has sheet-steel edges. Wear gloves.

steps.text: Unplug the ribbon cables from the main board and remove the board. Remove the power supply: an internal board or a brick behind a cover.
Remove the encoder strip: a clear plastic strip with fine lines running along the carriage. One end hooks onto a small tension spring; unhook it gently.
steps.warn: The spring flicks when released. Keep your face back.

steps.text: Release the belt: push the idler pulley at the far end toward the motor against its spring, and slip the belt off. Slide the carriage off the guide rod.
Remove the guide rod: undo the clips or screws at each end and slide it out.
Undo the carriage motor (2–3 screws, at one end of the rail) and the paper-feed motor (side frame). Keep any encoder disc and sensor with each motor.
Take the paper-feed rollers on their steel shafts, the gear trains, springs and any small switches.
Leave the ink sponge pads in the base: they are soaked with ink.

notes:
## What's worth keeping and why

- **DC motors with encoders.** Small brushed motors, usually rated around 24–32 V, that also run slower on 12 V. With the encoder disc and sensor, a motor knows how far it has turned: the base for a closed-loop drive.
- **Stepper motors.** Older and larger printers use steppers for paper feed: precise positioning for trackers and small machines.
- **Guide rod.** Polished, hardened steel rod, about 6–10 mm across. Axles, slides, hinge pins.
- **Timing belt and pulleys.** Toothed belt for linear motion without slip.
- **Encoder strip and sensor.** An optical sensor that reads fine lines; also works as a simple slot sensor.
- **Power supply.** Usually 24–32 V DC at under 2 A; some printers give two outputs. Good for driving the motors you just pulled, or step down to 12 V or 5 V with a buck converter.
- **Rubber rollers, gears, springs, screws.**

## Variations

- Small home printers use plastic frames and mostly DC motors. Larger office and wide-format printers have steel frames, larger steppers and heavier rods.
- Laser printers and copiers are a different job: heavier, with a fuser that gets very hot and a toner dust mess. See copier.
- Scanner units in all-in-ones carry a CIS light bar (LEDs) and a small stepper or DC motor.

## What to leave

- Ink cartridges, the print head and the waste ink pads.
- Small plastic parts with no clear use.
